newsitem.title: USA: Mass. lawmakers study how to end county government.
newsitem.headline: Mass. lawmakers study how to end county government.

text.p: About 20 Massachusetts representatives met behind closed doors on Monday trying to find out what assets fiscally-pressed Middlesex County has left.
Meanwhile on the Senate side of Beacon Hill, members were studying a proposal that would completely eliminate county government in the commonwealth over three fiscal years.

Unlike other states, Massachusetts county government has few means of generating revenues and provides little in the way of services and Middlesex County, the state's largest, defaulted on $4.5 million of revenue anticipation notes Friday.
Now, the Senate is considering a proposal that would abolish eight county governments as of Dec. 31 1998 and establish a regional government instead transferring all county debt to state.

The proposal, authored by Sen. Richard Moore whose district encompasses parts of Worcester and Norfolk counties, suggests transferring county employees to the state payroll and freezing hiring at the county level after Jan 1, 1997.
Gov. William Weld proposed eliminating county government during the Legislature's 1995 session, but the measure was defeated.
Middlesex County, home to Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, defaulted Friday after the state refused to allow the county to borrow more money.
The county, which has a nearly $23 million budget, ran into into trouble with its county hospital which recently has been operating at just 25 percent capacity.

It has agreed to sell the facility to for-profit Olympus Healthcare Group Inc. of Westborough, Mass. for $4.4 million, but that will not be enough to cover the county's $17 million in hospital-associated liabilities.
Rep. Bob Hargraves, who represents part of Middlesex County, blames the lack of accountability on the part of county commissioners for the financial problems.
"Nobody knows who their county commissioners are. These guys just keep getting elected over and over and nobody holds their feet to the fire," Hargraves said.
The default "is providing a catalyst to really look at the county government and see what can be done," he said.
Middlesex County officials did not return phone calls on Monday.
Defaults in the nation's $1.3 trillion municipal bond market are extremely rare, variously estimated at about one or two percent of the overall market.

Even beleaguered Orange County, Calif., which filed for bankrupty protection in December 1994, reached agreement with its noteholders to roll over its debt. Orange County, which emerged from bankruptcy earlier this year, said that meant it had not actually defaulted, though rating agency analysts disagreed on the distinction.
